Robustness Implies Weak Stability of Alg with a Randomized Outlier Rate Consider the lack of stability of the above inefficient algorithm: as written, there must be two adjacent Y, Y 0 such that Alg rejects on Y but not on Y 0 . We therefore introduce our first simple idea to patch the algorithm to prevent it from displaying such “drastic” change in its behavior. Randomizing the outlier rate The following is a simple but useful observation: If Alg does not reject on input Y with outlier rate η, then, Alg must also not reject on Y 0 outlier rate η + 1/n. To see why, let X be the set of points with subgaussian fourth moments that intersects Y in (1−η)n points. Then, since Y and Y 0 differ in at most one point, Y 0 must intersect X in at least (1 − η)n − 1 = (1 − (η + 1/n))n points. Thus, if, instead of a fixed outlier rate η, we ran Alg above with an appropriately “randomized” outlier rate, we might expect the rejection probabilities of Alg on Y, Y 0 to be similar. We can formalize this with a simple truncated Laplace noise injection procedure. Robustness implies weak stability in Mahalanobis norms We now consider whether the estimates computed on Y, Y 0 (assuming Alg does not reject on Y, Y 0 ) are close. First note that the outlier robustness of Alg already ensures a weak stability property. Specifically, suppose X, X 0 are the sets of size n generated by Alg when run on inputs Y, Y 0 . Then, since Y ∩ Y 0 is of size n − 1, |X ∩ X 0 | ⩾ (1 − 2η)n − 1. Next, observe that intersection bound above is equivalent to the uniform distributions on X, X 0 having a total variation distance of at most 2η + 1/n. Thus, from Fact 4, we know that the parameters of X, X 0 are O(η O(1) ) close in the relative Mahalanobis distance defined above. Thus we obtain stability properties in the right norms directly! However, this is a weak stability guarantee since it only provides a fixed constant distance guarantee instead of on (1) that one may expect given that Y and Y 0 differ in at most 1 out of n points. Nevertheless, our discussion shows that robustness, via the inefficient algorithm above, immediately implies weak stability. 2.3. Stabilizing the entropy potential: private stable selection Before describing our key idea, we first make a simple observation: Fix an input Y and consider the optimum value of the entropy potential of Alg when run with outlier rate η. What happens if we change η to η + 1/n? Clearly, the potential cannot increase: any solution ζ with outlier rate η is also a solution for outlier rate η + 1/n. The potential can decrease arbitrarily though. More specifically, we show that to make the entropy potential stable under a change of Y to an adjacent Y 0 , it suffices to run Y with an outlier rate η 0 = O(η) such that the entropy potential of Alg on Y for any outlier rate in [η 0 − L/n, η 0 + L/n] is within an additive O(L/n) e of any other. 0 To see why this claim could be true, informally speaking, observe that if Y is obtained from Y by changing at most a single point, then a solution ζ with outlier rate η 0 can be modified into a solution ζ 0 for Y 0 with outlier rate η 0 + 1/n by simply zeroing out the wi for the index i where Y 0 and Y differ. This allows us to relate the potentials for neighboring outlier rates on Y and Y 0 . Under the above assumption, the potential remains stable in an interval around η 0 on Y . This allows us to conclude that the same must be true for Y 0 for the interval [η 0 − L/n + 1, η 0 + L/n − 1]. The above reasoning allows us to obtain strong stability guarantees if we can 1) show that a stable interval as above exists and 2) find such an interval via a stable process. A stable selection procedure via the exponential mechanism We show that a stable interval as above (for L = O en (1)) exists via a simple Markov-like argument. Using an appropriate scoring rule, we show that the standard exponential mechanism can then be used to produce a stable interval like above via a stable algorithm (see Section A.6.4). Putting things together Altogether, we obtain a version of Alg that outputs a sequence of weights (i.e., Eζ [wi ]) that are stable under the modification of a single point in Y .
